**When people hear about an outbreak, some of them go and get vaccinated. How much does that slow the outbreak down, and what limits it?**

Most of a Starsim model is declared: its states and transitions, interventions, and results. Declared parts run under every solver, and `describe()`, `diagram()`, and `equations()` show them. But some things are easier to say in code: a rule of behavior, a quantity with its own dynamics, or a result of your own. A **module written as code** is a Python class with a `step()` method, which Starsim calls at each step, and which can read and change the rest of the sim, alongside the declared diseases.

A module that keeps only numbers for the whole population, like the one in the first half of this tutorial, runs with the rest of the model as an ODE. A module that keeps a value for each person needs agents: the second half writes a disease, a quantity for each person, and a network as code. By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

- write a function that Starsim calls at each step, and say when a class is needed instead;
- write a module as a class, with parameters, a state of its own, and results;
- read the model's results and move people between states from a module, in a way that works under every solver;
- compare scenarios that differ in a module's parameters;
- write a disease, a quantity for each person, and a network as code, for agents;
- choose between declaring part of a model and writing it as code.

Before writing a module, check the table at the top of [Custom modules](../user_guide/building_modules.qmd): many things that seem to need code (vaccination, testing, treatment, contact tracing, and changes to parameters) can be declared.

## The model so far

This is the measles model from [T6 – Data and calibration](t6_data.qmd), with the fitted values: β = 0.16, and 40% of infections reported. It runs for a year from 1 January, in a town of 100,000 people in three age groups, about 11% of them susceptible:

```{python}
import starsim as ss

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ 0.16*I         # β = 0.16 per contact per day
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)   # Latent for 10 days on average
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)    # Infectious for 8 days on average
cases       = ss.outcome(0.4*infection) # Reported cases: 40% of infections
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, cases,
    init = dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])), # The share immune in each age group
    init_n = dict(I=10),                          # 10 people infectious at the start
    name = 'measles',
)
measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}) # Ages 0-14, 15-64, and 65+

contacts = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[10, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]]) # Contacts a day, between age groups
settings = dict(networks=contacts, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01')

sim = ss.Sim(measles, **settings)
sim.run()
sim.plot('measles.cases')
```

## Vaccine demand

During measles outbreaks, parents who had put off vaccinating hear about cases and go to a clinic: an unplanned intervention the model leaves out. A simple rule: the rate at which susceptible people seek vaccination rises with the cases reported in the last week, reaching half its highest value (10% a week) at 300 cases a week.

The smallest module written as code is a function of the sim, called once each step; given as `interventions=`, it becomes an intervention. In it, `sim.results` has the results so far, and `sim.ti` is the index of the current time point. `ss.move()` moves people between a declared disease's states, the same way under every solver: here, those vaccinated and protected (93%) from `S` to `R`. A rate becomes the chance of an event in one step with `to_prob()`; written out, that is 1 − exp(−rate × dt):

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
def vaccine_demand(sim):
    """ The unvaccinated seek vaccination at a rate that rises with the cases reported in the last week """
    measles = sim.diseases.measles
    last_week = sim.results.measles.cases[max(sim.ti-7, 0):sim.ti].sum()      # Cases reported in the last 7 days
    share = last_week/(last_week + 300)                                       # From 0 to 1, a half at 300 cases a week
    seeking = (ss.perweek(0.1)*share).to_prob(sim.t.dt)                       # The chance of seeking vaccination in this step
    ss.move(measles.S, measles.R, p=seeking*0.93)                             # Those vaccinated and protected become immune
    return
```

## Explicit

```{python}
import numpy as np

def vaccine_demand(sim):
    """ The unvaccinated seek vaccination at a rate that rises with the cases reported in the last week """
    measles = sim.diseases.measles
    last_week = sim.results.measles.cases[max(sim.ti-7, 0):sim.ti].sum()      # Cases reported in the last 7 days
    share = last_week/(last_week + 300)                                       # From 0 to 1, a half at 300 cases a week
    rate = 0.1/7*share                                                        # The rate of seeking vaccination, per day
    seeking = 1 - np.exp(-rate*sim.t.dt.days)                                 # The chance of seeking vaccination in this step
    ss.move(measles.S, measles.R, p=seeking*0.93)                             # Those vaccinated and protected become immune
    return
```
:::

```{python}
sims = {
    'No response': ss.Sim(measles, **settings),
    'Vaccine demand': ss.Sim(measles, interventions=vaccine_demand, **settings),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
print('Solver:', msim.sims['Vaccine demand'].solver)
msim.plot('measles.I')
```

The sim still runs as an ODE, since the function keeps nothing for each person, and demand makes the outbreak smaller. But the function's numbers are fixed inside it, it has no results (so how many doses were given?), and it forgets a case abruptly after 7 days, which isn't how people remember news.

## A module as a class

A module written as a class fixes all three. It inherits from one of Starsim's module types (here `ss.Intervention`), so that it runs at the right point in each step and ends up in the right place on the sim:

| Base class | Use for | Added to the sim via |
|---|---|---|
| `ss.Disease`, `ss.AgentDisease` | Disease natural history and transmission | `diseases=` |
| `ss.Network` | Who contacts whom | `networks=` |
| `ss.Demographics` | Births, deaths, migration | `demographics=` |
| `ss.Intervention` | Actions that change the simulation | `interventions=` |
| `ss.Analyzer` | Recording results without changing anything | `analyzers=` |
| `ss.Connector` | Interactions between modules | `connectors=` |
| `ss.Module` | Anything that doesn't fit the others | `modules=` (or as a positional argument) |

The module has:

- **Parameters**, with defaults in `__init__()` via `define_pars()`, changed by name when the module is made (`update_pars()` raises an error for an unknown name, catching misspellings). Rates and durations are Starsim [time parameters](../user_guide/building_time.qmd) (e.g. `ss.days(30)`, `ss.perweek(0.1)`), so they mean the same whatever the step length.
- **A state of its own**: here, one number for the whole population, the cases people remember. It is a memory that fades: each step adds the new reported cases and forgets a share of what is remembered, so a case is remembered for `memory` (30 days) on average. This is a small ODE of the module's own, dM/dt = cases − M/memory, solved a step at a time.
- **Results of its own**, defined in `init_results()` with `define_results()`, and filled in each step at `self.ti`. `kind='flow'` says doses are events in each step (summed over time), and `kind='stock'` that the cases remembered are a quantity at each time point.
- **A `step()` method**, which does the work. In it, `self.sim` is the sim, `self.t.dt` the step length, and `self.pars` the parameters.

A module can also limit what it does: here, clinics can give at most `capacity` doses a day (no limit by default), and people who can't be served stay susceptible and try again the next day:

```{python}
class VaccineDemand(ss.Intervention):
    """ Unvaccinated people seek vaccination at a rate that rises with the outbreak cases they remember """

    def __init__(self, memory=ss.days(30), half=300, max_rate=ss.perweek(0.1), capacity=None, efficacy=0.93, **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_pars(
            memory   = memory,   # How long a reported case is remembered, on average
            half     = half,     # The number of cases remembered at which demand is half its highest
            max_rate = max_rate, # The highest rate at which unvaccinated people seek vaccination
            capacity = capacity, # The most doses the clinics can give, as a rate (None for no limit)
            efficacy = efficacy, # The share of those vaccinated who are protected
        )
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)
        self.remembered = 0.0 # The cases that people remember, for the whole population
        return

    def init_results(self):
        super().init_results()
        self.define_results(
            ss.Result('doses', kind='flow', scale=False, label='Doses given'),
            ss.Result('remembered', kind='stock', scale=False, label='Cases remembered'),
        )
        return

    def step(self):
        measles = self.sim.diseases.measles
        dt = self.t.dt

        # Remember the cases reported in the last step, and forget a share of those remembered
        new_cases = self.sim.results.measles.cases[self.ti-1]
        self.remembered += new_cases - self.remembered*(dt/self.pars.memory)

        # The doses sought, limited by what the clinics can give
        share = self.remembered/(self.remembered + self.pars.half)
        seeking = (self.pars.max_rate*share).to_prob(dt)
        doses = seeking*measles.S.n
        if self.pars.capacity is not None:
            doses = min(doses, self.pars.capacity.to_events(dt))

        # Those protected become immune
        ss.move(measles.S, measles.R, n=doses*self.pars.efficacy)
        self.results.doses[self.ti] = doses
        self.results.remembered[self.ti] = self.remembered
        return
```

`measles.S.n` is the number of people in `S` now, under every solver, and `ss.move(..., n=...)` moves a number of people rather than a share. `self.sim.results.measles.cases[self.ti-1]` is the last step's reported cases: a module that is not a disease steps before the diseases, so this step's cases aren't known yet. The sim runs as an ODE, as before. The module is named after its class in lower case, so its results are in `sim.results.vaccinedemand`.

## Comparing scenarios

With parameters, one module serves every scenario: no response (a highest rate of 0), demand met in full, and clinics that can give at most 30 doses a day, about what a few clinics in a town of 100,000 might manage on top of their usual work:

```{python}
sims = {
    'No response':           ss.Sim(measles, interventions=VaccineDemand(max_rate=ss.perweek(0)), **settings),
    'Demand met in full':    ss.Sim(measles, interventions=VaccineDemand(), **settings),
    'At most 30 doses a day': ss.Sim(measles, interventions=VaccineDemand(capacity=ss.perday(30)), **settings),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot(['measles.I', 'vaccinedemand.doses'])
```

```{python}
msim.summarize().loc[['measles_infection', 'vaccinedemand_doses']]
```

With demand met in full, the outbreak infects about 5,400 people rather than 9,400: about 4,900 doses prevent about 4,000 infections. Doses peak in mid-March, during the steep rise, when each person protected breaks the most chains of infection; after that, fewer people are left to seek a dose. With at most 30 doses a day, clinics run at capacity from late February to late April, and people waiting in March, when it matters most, are often infected: about 6,600 in all, with fewer doses given. Even met in full, demand prevents less than half of the infections, because it starts only once the outbreak is under way; vaccination before an outbreak, or a campaign at its start ([T5](t5_interventions.qmd)), doesn't wait.

`sim.describe()` lists the module, but can't say what it does, since that is in its code: the cost of writing part of a model as code. A module's parameters can be fitted to data ([T6](t6_data.qmd#fitting-and-checking-the-fit)) if given as `ss.par` with bounds, e.g. `VaccineDemand(half=ss.par(300, bounds=[50, 2000]))`.

## What changes with a module written as code

- **The solver.** A module that keeps only numbers for the whole population runs under every solver. A module that keeps a value for each person (a state made with `define_states()`) runs only as agents, and a sim with one runs as agents by itself, its declared diseases unchanged: see [below](#a-quantity-for-each-person-immunity-that-fades). If a module asks for individual people (e.g. `measles.I.uids`) in a run without agents, the run stops and says so.
- **The order.** In each step, a module that is not a disease runs before the diseases, so what it does applies to the same step's transmission, and it sees the previous step's results.
- **The sim's own copy.** The sim works on its own copy of each module, so from a module, reach others through `self.sim` in `step()` (e.g. `self.sim.diseases.measles`), not a variable from outside the class.

[Custom modules](../user_guide/building_modules.qmd) covers the rest: the other kinds of module (analyzers, connectors, networks, demographics, and diseases written as code), states for each person, the order in which Starsim calls a module's methods, and the pitfalls. [Analyzers](../user_guide/interventions_analyzers.qmd) covers modules that record something without changing the model.

## Modules for individual people

A model of individual people sometimes needs something declarations can't say: a quantity each person carries that changes continuously, your own rule for who meets whom, or a disease whose course is easiest to say step by step.

The rest of this tutorial writes the kinds of module that agent-based models most often need:

1. **A disease written as code**: the waning immunity of [T3](t3_disease.qmd#counting-each-persons-infections), as Starsim 3 wrote it, to compare with the declared version.
2. **A quantity for each person**: immunity that fades gradually, which a declared model can't say, in a module of its own.
3. **A network written as code**: contacts with people of a similar age.

Each trades some of what Starsim knows about the model (what `describe()` can show, which solvers can run it) for freedom.

## A disease written as code

In [T3](t3_disease.qmd#counting-each-persons-infections), waning immunity was one more declared transition, `R >> S`. Here is the same SIRS model written as code. The easiest approach is to inherit from a template and change only what differs. `ssl.AgentSIR` is the SIR model written as code (Starsim 3's `ss.SIR`); its states are per-agent arrays, `susceptible`, `infected`, and `recovered`, and its methods move agents between them:

```{python}
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import starsim.library as ssl

class SIRS(ssl.AgentSIR):
    def __init__(self, pars=None, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_pars(
            dur_imm = ss.expon(mean=ss.days(180)), # How long immunity lasts after recovery
        )
        self.update_pars(pars, **kwargs)

        # SIR states are added automatically; here we add the time of losing immunity
        self.define_states(
            ss.TimeArr('ti_susceptible', label='Time of becoming susceptible again'),
        )
        return

    def set_progression(self, uids):
        """ Schedule recovery and death as usual, then schedule the waning of immunity """
        super().set_progression(uids)
        recovering = uids[np.isfinite(self.ti_recovered[uids])] # Agents who are going to die have ti_recovered = NaN
        self.ti_susceptible[recovering] = self.ti_recovered[recovering] + self.pars.dur_imm.rvs(recovering)
        return

    def step_state(self):
        """ Do the usual SIR transitions, then return agents whose immunity has waned to susceptible """
        super().step_state()
        waning = (self.recovered & self.ti_susceptible.due()).uids # Those whose time has come
        self.recovered[waning] = False
        self.susceptible[waning] = True
        return
```

The changes are:

1. `__init__()` adds the extra parameter (`dur_imm`) and state (`ti_susceptible`); the SIR states are inherited.
2. `ssl.AgentSIR.set_prognoses()` calls `set_infection()` to make agents infectious, then `set_progression()` to schedule what happens next. Only the second needs extending: `super()` does the usual scheduling, then a waning time is drawn for everyone who will recover (those who will die have `ti_recovered` set to `NaN`).
3. `step_state()` likewise calls `super()` and adds only the recovered → susceptible transition.

Here it is next to the declared SIRS of T3, with the same R0 (0.4 per day × 7 days = 2.8) and durations. A disease written as code transmits over the sim's networks, so both get a mixing pool with one contact a day each, the same as homogeneous mixing with β = 0.4 per day:

```{python}
coded = SIRS(beta=ss.perday(0.4), dur_inf=ss.expon(mean=ss.days(7)), p_death=0, init_prev=0.01, name='cold')

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
declared = ss.Disease(
    infection = S >> I @ 0.4*I,          # A chance of infection of 0.4 per contact per day
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(7),
    waning    = R >> S @ ss.days(180),
    init_prev = 0.01,
    name      = 'cold',
)

pars = dict(networks=ss.MixingPool(n_contacts=1), n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(2*365), verbose=0)
sim_coded = ss.Sim(coded, **pars)
sim_declared = ss.Sim(declared, **pars)
sim_coded.run()
sim_declared.run()

plt.figure()
plt.plot(sim_declared.results.cold.timevec, sim_declared.results.cold.I, label='Declared')
plt.plot(sim_coded.results.cold.timevec, sim_coded.results.cold.infected, label='Written as code')
plt.ylabel('Number infectious')
plt.legend();
```

The two are the same model, and give the same epidemic up to chance: a large first wave, then smaller waves as immunity wanes. They turn rates into chances and round durations to whole steps the same way, so averaged over a few seeds, their first waves peak within about 1% of each other. What differs is what Starsim knows about them. The declared disease can be shown (`describe()`, `diagram()`, `equations()`), run as an ODE or a stochastic compartmental model as well as agents, and fitted with `sim.fit()`; its results are named after its states and transitions. The coded one runs only as agents, and Starsim can't show what it does. So if a model can be declared, declare it. Write a disease as code when its course is easier to say in code, or to keep a Starsim 3 model as it was (a Starsim 3 subclass of `ss.SIR` can subclass `ssl.AgentSIR` unchanged).

## The parts of a module for agents

Besides the parameters, results, and `step()` of a [module as a class](#a-module-as-a-class), a module for agents often has:

- **States.** Per-agent arrays that persist across steps, declared with `self.define_states()`: `ss.BoolState` for true or false, `ss.FloatArr` for a number, and `ss.TimeArr` for a time, as a step number (`due()` gives those whose time has come, rounding at random in proportion so durations keep their mean). Each becomes an attribute (`self.ti_susceptible`) that grows as agents are born, and each `ss.BoolState` gives a result, the number for whom it is true. Keep per-agent data this way, never in a plain Python attribute or array.
- **When results are recorded.** Besides in `step()`, a stock (the state at the start of the step) can be recorded in `record_stocks()`, and a flow (what happened in the step) in `record_flows()`.
- **Randomness.** Use a Starsim distribution (e.g. `ss.expon`, `ss.bernoulli`, `ss.normal`), not `np.random`, so results stay reproducible and scenarios differ only where they should; see [Random numbers](../user_guide/mechanics_random.qmd).

## A quantity for each person: immunity that fades

Above, immunity is all or nothing: full protection until people move back to S, then none. For many respiratory infections, protection fades gradually as antibodies decline, so susceptibility depends on how long ago each person recovered. A per-person quantity that changes continuously can't be declared, but takes a few lines of code.

The module holds each person's antibody level, 1 just after recovery and halving every `half_life`. It is an `ss.Module`, being neither a disease nor an intervention, and reads who recovered in the last step from the declared disease (`recovery.uids`):

```{python}
class Antibodies(ss.Module):
    """ Each person's antibody level: 1 on recovery, then halving every half_life """

    def __init__(self, half_life=ss.days(90), **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_pars(
            half_life = half_life,
        )
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)
        self.define_states(
            ss.FloatArr('level', default=0.0, label='Antibody level'),
        )
        return

    def init_results(self):
        super().init_results()
        self.define_results(
            ss.Result('mean_level', label='Mean antibody level', kind='ratio'), # A mean (a ratio), so not scaled by the number of people per agent
        )
        return

    def step(self):
        decay = 0.5**(self.t.dt/self.pars.half_life) # The share left after one step
        self.level[:] = self.level*decay
        recovered = self.sim.diseases.cold.recovery.uids # Those who recovered in the last step
        self.level[recovered] = 1.0
        return

    def record_stocks(self): # At the start of each step, so each value is the level at its time point
        super().record_stocks()
        self.results.mean_level[self.ti] = self.level.mean()
        return
```

The infection itself is SIS (people go back to S when they recover), so the antibodies are its only protection. The module keeps the level, and a modifier multiplies each person's susceptibility by what the antibodies leave of it. A modifier never overwrites what it changes, so the disease's own `rel_sus` is kept, and `describe()` lists the modifier as part of the model:

```{python}
S, I = ss.states('S I')
sis = ss.Disease(infection=S >> I @ 0.4*I, recovery=I >> S @ ss.days(7), init_prev=0.01, name='cold')

def susceptibility(sim):
    """ Each person's susceptibility: 1 minus their antibody level """
    return 1 - sim.custom.antibodies.level

protection = ss.modify(sis.rel_sus, multiply=susceptibility)
```

Here are the infection with antibodies that halve every 90 days, with no immunity, and the all-or-nothing SIRS, whose protection lasts 180 days on average (about two half-lives):

```{python}
sims = {
    'No immunity':          ss.Sim(sis, **pars),
    'All or nothing':       ss.Sim(declared, **pars),
    'Antibodies that fade': ss.Sim(sis, Antibodies(), connectors=protection, **pars),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('cold.I')
```

With no immunity, the infection settles at once at an endemic level. With either kind of immunity, the first wave leaves many people protected, so cases fall and then rise again as protection is lost. With fading antibodies, people regain some susceptibility soon after recovering, so the second wave comes sooner and is larger, and the endemic level is about twice that with all-or-nothing immunity. The module's own result is in the sim's results, under its name:

```{python}
msim.sims['Antibodies that fade'].results.antibodies.mean_level.plot()
```

A module that keeps a value for each person needs agents, so a sim with one runs as agents, including its declared diseases, unchanged.

## A network written as code

The networks of [T4](t4_mixing.qmd#contacts-per-person) pair people at random, or as partners. Suppose instead that people mostly meet others of a similar age. A network written as code subclasses `ss.Network` (or one of its subclasses) and overrides how edges are made: `add_pairs()` makes them, and `step()`, called every step, here replaces the day's contacts. `self.append()` adds edges, as the UIDs of the two people in each (`p1` and `p2`) and a transmission multiplier (`beta`).

To pair people of similar ages, sort them by age plus a little random noise (standard deviation `spread`), and connect each person with their neighbors in that order:

```{python}
class AgeNet(ss.Network):
    """ Contacts each day with people close in age """

    def __init__(self, n_contacts=4, spread=ss.years(2), **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_pars(
            n_contacts = n_contacts, # The number of contacts each person has each day (an even number)
            spread = spread,         # How far apart in age contacts tend to be
        )
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)
        self.noise = ss.normal(0, 1) # A Starsim distribution, so that the draws are reproducible
        return

    def add_pairs(self):
        uids = self.sim.people.alive.uids
        age = self.sim.people.age[uids] + self.pars.spread.years*self.noise.rvs(uids) # Each person's age, blurred a little
        order = uids[np.argsort(age, kind='stable')] # Everyone, from youngest to oldest
        p1, p2 = [], []
        for k in range(1, self.pars.n_contacts//2 + 1): # Each person, with the k-th next person in the order
            p1.append(order[:-k])
            p2.append(order[k:])
        p1 = np.concatenate(p1)
        p2 = np.concatenate(p2)
        self.append(p1=p1, p2=p2, weight=np.ones(len(p1)))
        return

    def step(self):
        self.remove_edges(np.ones(len(self), dtype=bool)) # Yesterday's contacts end...
        self.add_pairs()                                  # ...and today's begin
        return
```

Check that a network makes what you meant: here, contacts should be of nearly the same age, about 4 per person:

```{python}
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
cold = ss.Disease(infection=S >> I @ 0.1*I, # A chance of infection of 0.1 per contact per day: with 4 contacts, R0 = 0.1 × 4 × 7 = 2.8
                   recovery=I >> R @ ss.days(7), init_prev=0.001, name='cold')

pars = dict(n_agents=5000, stop=ss.days(250), verbose=0)
sim = ss.Sim(cold, networks=AgeNet(), **pars)
sim.init()
df = sim.networks.agenet.to_df()
age = sim.people.age
print('Correlation of the ages of contacts:', round(np.corrcoef(age[ss.uids(df.p1)], age[ss.uids(df.p2)])[0, 1], 3))
print('Contacts per person:', round(2*len(df)/len(sim.people), 2))
```

Now compare it with a random network with the same number of contacts:

```{python}
sims = {
    'Random contacts':       ss.Sim(cold, networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=4), **pars),
    'Contacts close in age': ss.Sim(cold, networks=AgeNet(), **pars),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('cold.I')
```

With the same number of contacts, contacts close in age give a slower, flatter epidemic that reaches about as many people: each case's contacts overlap with those of whoever infected them, so the infection can't jump across the population. A contact matrix with many narrow age groups would give much the same, under every solver ([T4](t4_mixing.qmd#contacts-between-age-groups)); a network written as code is worth it when the rule is about individuals, such as who is in which household, school, or partnership.

## Which to use

| | What you write | What Starsim still does | What is given up |
|---|---|---|---|
| Declared | States, transitions, deliveries, modifiers | Everything: `describe()`, every solver, fitting | Nothing, if it can say what you need |
| Declared, with a little code | A function of the sim as a rate, a condition, or a modifier's amount | Results, solvers that can take the function, fitting | Speed (the function runs once a step), and showing what the function does |
| A module written as code | A class with `step()` (and states, results, parameters) | Time, people, random numbers, parallel runs, its results | Showing what the module does, and solvers other than agents if it keeps a value for each person |
| A disease or network written as code | A subclass of `ss.AgentDisease` or `ss.Network` | The same, and transmission over the sim's networks | The same, and fitting its structure |

Start declared, and move down the table only for the part that needs it. Here, the SIRS model needed no code; the antibodies needed a module only for the level itself; and the network needed code for its rule of who meets whom. When code is slow because it loops over agents, `@ss.jit` compiles a function with Numba; see [Custom modules](../user_guide/building_modules.qmd), which also covers the order in which Starsim calls a module's methods, demographics and connectors written as code, and pitfalls.

## Exercises

1. How much does it matter how long people remember cases? Run `VaccineDemand()` with a memory of 10 days and of 90 days, and compare the infections and doses with 30 days. Does each extra dose prevent as many infections as the ones before? Why not?
2. People who hear about an outbreak may also avoid others. Add a modifier, `ss.modify(measles.rel_sus, multiply=...)`, whose `multiply=` is a function of the sim returning 1 − 0.3 × the share used for demand (so contacts fall by up to 30%), reading the cases remembered as `sim.interventions.vaccinedemand.remembered`. How much smaller is the outbreak?
3. Run the model with demand met in full as agents, one for each person (`n_agents=100_000`), and compare the infections and doses with those of the ODE. Does the module need any change? Why not?
4. Change the half-life of the antibodies to 30 days and to 365 days. How does each change the endemic level of infection, compared with no immunity and with the all-or-nothing SIRS?
5. Give `AgeNet` a parameter `p_random`, the share of each person's contacts that are with anyone at random rather than with people close in age (hint: shuffle a share of the order before pairing, or add a second, random network). How large does it have to be before the epidemic looks like the one with random contacts?
6. The `SIRS` class schedules each person's loss of immunity at recovery. Write an `SIRS` in which immunity is lost instead with a constant chance each step (an exponential duration, drawn step by step), using an `ss.bernoulli` distribution in `step_state()`. Does it give the same epidemic?

## Further reading

- [Funk et al. (2010): Modelling the influence of human behaviour on the spread of infectious diseases: a review](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20504800/): models in which people respond to an epidemic, as here
- [EpiModel: Extending EpiModel](https://epimodel.github.io/EpiModel-Gallery/): worked examples of modules of your own, for network models
- [Mesa: Introductory tutorial](https://mesa.readthedocs.io/latest/tutorials/0_first_model.html): writing a model of your own as code, step by step, in another Python framework
- [NetworkX: graph generators](https://networkx.org/documentation/stable/reference/generators.html): ready-made graphs that can be turned into a Starsim network (`ssl.StaticNet`)
- [Numba: a 5-minute guide](https://numba.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user/5minguide.html): compiling Python loops, as `@ss.jit` does
